The Almohad Caliphate. From 1121 to 1269 of the common era, this was a North African Berber dynasty that emerged as a reformist reaction against the Almoravids, calling for a return to strict monotheistic doctrine and tawhid—God's oneness. Rising from the Atlas Mountains under Muhammad ibn Tumart, the Almohads became vastly more powerful than their predecessors, controlling both the Maghreb and Spain at their zenith before fragmenting into successor states.

The Almohads were founded by Muhammad ibn Tumart, who died in 1130, as a theological and political movement emphasizing rigorous monotheism. He rejected what he saw as Almoravid drift from pure Islamic doctrine. His successor, Abd al-Mu'min, consolidated power and transformed the movement into an empire starting in 1147, conquering Almoravid territories across North Africa and Spain within a generation. At their height in the late twelfth century, they controlled Spain and the Maghreb simultaneously, making them the geographically largest Berber empire—though Spain gradually slipped away to the Christian Reconquista. Despite their surface orthodoxy, the Almohads patronized architecture and learning. They funded monumental mosques and the transmission of Greek philosophy through Averroes and Maimonides. They maintained a theocratic state apparatus where the caliph was both political and spiritual head, claiming descent from Prophet Muhammad to strengthen legitimacy. After 1212, following military defeats in Spain, they fragmented. By 1269 they had been replaced by smaller dynasties like the Marinids in the Maghreb and the Nasrids in Granada.

The Almoravid Dynasty came before them, and the Almohads overthrew and superseded them. Islamic Spanish territories in Al-Andalus were where their rule was most contested. The philosopher Averroes was patronized under their rule. And the Jewish thinker and doctor Maimonides flourished in their lands.
